title: Limit the load of each step
statement: Limit what each step asks a reader to hold: few new names per section, few short options per item, no long reading without a check, each task on one screen.
example: A scan of one course found 137 of 772 items over a five-option cap.
detail: Reviews of a Grade 5 course flagged a ~204-word part that introduced eight new proper names before an item asked students to compare four options of ~50–70 words each, and four consecutive reading pages with no interaction (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-08-19.md`, `grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-08-19-R2.md`). A simulated outside review of four Grade 3 lessons found 3 narrated passage chunks, of 241, 273 and 279 words, that kept students passive for more than 60 seconds before a check (`grade3-reading/artifacts/arc-audit/SIM-REVIEW-D7-D8-D10-D12.md`). An outside review of a Grade 3 course called one item's twelve selectable options an excessive motor and cognitive load for an eight-year-old (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5_build_2026_07_02/feedback_clean.md`); a scan of a Grade 5 course found 137 of 772 items over a cap of 5 (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-merged-course/option_cap_report.md`), and a one-screen census found tasks running past the fold at 1440×900 and split them (`grade3-reading/artifacts/qc-run-2026-09-04/`).

- **W-11. WORTH-FIXING — four consecutive reading pages with no interaction

evidence.quote: ### 3. HIGH — one-screen census, our lane (additions row I/census)
**Rule of thumb (declared, not measured):** at G3, a single lesson introduces **≤ ~5 new allusive/vocabulary anchors**, and a unit spirals them rather than front-loading.
its **G3 delivery cap** is the tightest; the same topic can spend more of its density at G6+.
